text: If depth helps, a deeper network should never be worse than a shallower one, because the extra layers could simply learn to pass their input through unchanged. Yet in 2015, Kaiming He and colleagues found that plain networks of fifty-six layers had higher training error than networks of twenty. The problem was not overfitting, since training error itself got worse; the deeper networks were simply harder to optimise.

Their fix was the residual connection. Instead of asking a block of layers to produce its output from scratch, we add the block's input back to its output, so the block computes x plus F of x. The layers now only need to learn F, the change to make, which is called the residual. It is like editing a document with tracked changes rather than retyping it: if nothing needs changing, the layers can learn to output zero, and the block passes its input straight through.

The deeper reason it works lies in backpropagation. Recall that addition passes its gradient through unchanged. Because the block adds x to F of x, the gradient arriving at the output flows back to x directly along the shortcut, as well as through the layers. Even if the gradient through the layers becomes tiny, the shortcut carries the signal back intact, so every block, however deep, receives a usable learning signal.

There is one practical requirement: x and F of x must have the same shape, or they cannot be added. When a block changes the number of channels or halves the size of the image, the shortcut applies a small projection, often a one by one convolution, so that the shapes match again.

The results were dramatic. Residual networks over a hundred layers deep won the ImageNet competition in 2015, and the same paper trained a network of more than a thousand layers on a smaller dataset. Depth, which had been a liability, became something a designer could simply choose.

Every transformer is built around this idea. Each block reads the token vectors, computes an update with attention or with a feed-forward network, and adds that update back, so the vectors flow through the model along a single path that people call the residual stream, with each block writing its contribution into it. Without residual connections, models dozens of blocks deep would be very hard to train.

So a residual connection adds a block's input to its output, letting the layers learn only the change and giving gradients a direct path home. That completes our tour of convolutional networks; next we turn to language itself, starting with how text becomes tokens.
